Choosing an analysis for clustered binary outcomes when clusters are few and series are short: a simulation study and two clinical applications

Abstract

For binary outcomes measured repeatedly on few subjects, small-sample sandwich corrections have been evaluated mainly by number of clusters, rarely by number of occasions. We compared strategies for a within-subject treatment-by-time interaction over 2,376 design points (10-145 clusters, 2-10 occasions, four mechanisms, one purely serial) and in subsamples of two clinical datasets. With t references, only the marginalized multilevel model with a convergence check had no design point clearly above 7.5% type I error among strategies with an interval, although a replication could flag a few; it answered in 84% of datasets. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) with first-order autoregressive working correlation and the Fay-Graubard correction answered in 92% and were closer to nominal at ten clusters with more occasions, but were clearly above 7.5% at 2 design points with ten clusters and two occasions; every false positive there came from a plausible estimate on separated data, on which the marginalized model rarely answered. The mixed-model Wald test was anticonservative; with adaptive quadrature (random intercept) only with ten occasions. With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters both answered in under half of datasets; a sign-flip score test answered in 72% and kept its level, without an estimate. We recommend the marginalized model; Fay-Graubard corrected GEE, preceded by a check for separation, is a simpler alternative except with ten clusters and two occasions.

Keywords. clustered binary data; few clusters; sandwich variance; small-sample correction; marginalized multilevel model; estimand; simulation study.

1. Introduction

Binary outcomes measured repeatedly within clusters, such as observations within patients or zones within a lung, are analysed in one of three ways. A generalized estimating equation (GEE) targets a population-averaged contrast and treats the dependence as a nuisance. A generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) targets a cluster-specific contrast and models the dependence explicitly. A marginalized multilevel model (MMM) specifies both: a marginal mean model of scientific interest and a conditional model that generates the dependence [1,2]. In applied work the choice may follow the conventions of the field rather than evidence about the design at hand.

The three approaches target different quantities. Under a logit link the marginal and conditional contrasts differ. With a normal random intercept of variance \(\sigma^2\), the marginal contrast is approximately the conditional one multiplied by

\[\left(1 + k^2\sigma^2\right)^{-1/2}, \qquad k = \frac{16\sqrt{3}}{15\pi},\]

so the gap widens with the variance of the random effects [3]. A further difference arises when the two are adjusted for different covariate sets, because the odds ratio is not collapsible [4]. A method comparison can nevertheless score a mixed model against a marginal target it does not estimate.

This paper concerns designs with few clusters and short series, where the asymptotic arguments behind all three approaches are weakest. Cluster-randomized trials with ten to thirty clusters are common [5], and many stepped-wedge trials have fewer than ten [6]. The sandwich variance estimator is anticonservative with few clusters, and a family of small-sample corrections exists to repair it [7-9]. These corrections have been evaluated on clustered and longitudinal data [10-14], with as few as ten subjects and four occasions [12]. They have also been evaluated on parallel cluster-randomized trials [15], where the simulation evidence has been reviewed systematically [16] and whole analysis strategies have been compared [17], and on stepped-wedge trials with binary outcomes [18]. In the original evaluations of the corrections and in the cluster-randomized comparisons [7,9,15,19,20], the unit within a cluster is never a subject measured on several occasions. None of these studies fits a random slope, and only Fay and Graubard [9] generate random regression coefficients, as a misspecification check. Whether their recommendations hold with two or three occasions per subject has not been established.

We report a simulation study planned and reported following Morris, White and Crowther [21], and two clinical applications. The study has three components. The first is a simulation over four data-generating mechanisms and a grid that extends to ten clusters and two occasions. Three mechanisms contain a component that is constant within subject, as the methods compared assume, and the fourth has only serial dependence. One scenario takes its prevalence and between-subject variance from a neonatal lung-ultrasound cohort [22]. The second is a recommendation stated as a decision rule that must hold at every simulated design point. The third is a plasmode application to the cohort and to a public respiratory trial, each repeatedly subsampled into the few-cluster regime with the full-data estimate as reference.

2. Methods

The study is reported in the order aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures (ADEMP) [21]. The analysis reported here followed a protocol in this structure, versioned before any rerun and released with the code. Table 1 summarizes it. The full parameter table, extracted from the executed code, is in Table S1.

2.1 Aims

The aims concern the treatment-by-time interaction on the logit scale, in longitudinal binary data with few clusters and short series. We evaluated (i) the type I error of the test of no interaction; (ii) its power, raw and size-adjusted; (iii) bias, precision and confidence-interval coverage of the estimate against the estimand of each method; and (iv) the probability that a method returns a usable result. We also evaluated a sign-flip score test, which returns a p-value only, and the interval obtained by inverting it. The clinical applications and the decision rule of Section 2.6 build on these aims but are not simulation aims.

2.2 Data-generating mechanisms

Table 2 summarizes the four mechanisms and the scenarios; the full parameters are in Table S1. The main grid crossed 16 cluster counts, N ∈ {10, 15, 20, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75, 85, 95, 105, 115, 125, 135, 145}, with 6 maximum numbers of occasions, T ∈ {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10}. It also crossed five mean-model scenarios (M1-M5) and the first three mechanisms below, giving 1,440 design points, and the same five scenarios with the fourth mechanism (480 design points). Each design point was simulated under the alternative (H1) and the null (H0), and the two hypotheses differed only in the tested marginal coefficient. T is a maximum. Each subject was observed at all T occasions with probability 0.7, and otherwise at a number of occasions drawn uniformly from \(1\) to \(T-1\). At T = 2, between 29% and 31% of subjects therefore contributed a single observation. Treatment was assigned to subjects with probability 0.5.

The mean model of scenario M1 is \(\mathrm{logit}\,\mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 \mathrm{trt} + \beta_3\, t \times \mathrm{trt}\). Its marginal coefficients under H1 are (-2, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2), which give a marginal prevalence of about 0.14 at T = 2. M2 adds a subject-level covariate (age). M3 and M4 add a random slope on time; in GenBinaryY its counterpart is a latent standard deviation that changes over time. M4 uses a smaller interaction (0.05). M5 adds a second covariate that varies over time (dose), with its own random slope.

The four mechanisms differ in how the dependence is generated.

  1. GenBinaryY is a marginalized model with a latent variable and a first-order transition term [1,2,23], simulated with the function GenBinaryY of the R package MMLB [24]. The latent standard deviation is a linear predictor, which in M3-M5 grows by 0.01 per occasion. This is the mechanism of the marginalized model.
  2. GLMM-native is a logistic mixed model with normal random effects. The random intercept has variance 1 and, in M3-M5, the random slope on time has variance 0.001. The conditional coefficients are the marginal ones multiplied by 1.16 (1.49 in M1c). This is the mechanism of the mixed model.
  3. GLMM-AR1 adds a latent first-order autoregressive process to the random effects of GLMM-native (ρ = 0.6, variance 0.5). Its random intercept is still constant within subject.
  4. Copula-AR1 is a Gaussian copula with logistic margins. The latent normal scores of a subject have correlation \(\rho^{|t_j - t_k|}\), with ρ = 0.6, and no component is constant within subject. None of the likelihood-based methods compared models this mechanism.

A sixth scenario, M1c, simulated with the first three mechanisms, uses the mean model of M1 with the prevalence (0.59) and the between-subject variance (3.5) of the clinical cohort of Section 2.7. It covers 72 design points, with N up to 45 and T up to 6. Four further scenarios, M6 and M7 on GenBinaryY and on GLMM-native, test the convergence check of Section 2.4 where the latent variability grows strongly over time. They cover the full grid (384 design points).

The values of the main scenarios were compared with the clinical cohort of Section 2.7. Their marginal prevalence (0.14 at T = 2 and 0.28 at T = 10 in M1) is much lower than in the cohort (0.59), and their random-intercept variance (1) is lower than the patient variance of the cohort (3.5); scenario M1c was added for this reason. The cohort has no treatment and few patients with repeated timepoints, so the interaction per occasion has no direct anchor in it. The cumulative value of the simulated interaction at ten occasions (1.8 on the logit scale) is of the order of the regional contrasts estimated in the cohort, for example 1.1 between lateral and anterior zones.

Each design point received 1,000 replicates per hypothesis. Replicates in which one treatment arm was never observed after the first occasion were excluded from every denominator (247 per hypothesis on the main grid of each mechanism, 43 in M1c, and 47 and 55 in M6 and M7). Replicate i of scenario m used the seed 20260805 + 1000m + i under the L’Ecuyer-CMRG generator. The seed was the same for both hypotheses and for every N, T and mechanism, so the datasets are common random numbers across cells [21].

2.3 Estimands and true values

The estimand is the coefficient of the treatment-by-time interaction on the logit scale. It is marginal for the marginalized model, the GEEs and the shrinkage GLM, and conditional on the random effects for the mixed model. In GenBinaryY the marginal true value is the generating coefficient. There is no conditional true value, so bias and coverage of the mixed model are not defined on that mechanism. In GLMM-native the conditional true value is the generating coefficient. The marginal value was obtained by Gauss-Hermite quadrature on the realized design; under H0 it is not exactly zero, ranging from -0.0030 to -0.0011 across scenarios M1-M5 and T, and under H1 it ranges from 0.044 to 0.20 (0.19 to 0.20 in M1c). In GLMM-AR1 the marginal true value is the target, and the conditional value was computed for each replicate. In Copula-AR1 the marginal true value is the generating coefficient, and there is no conditional true value.

2.4 Methods compared

The eight methods of Table 3 and the further strategies of Table 1 were applied to every dataset. The marginalized multilevel model was fitted with MMLB::mm [24] (20 quadrature points), with the latent-variable and transition formulas of the GenBinaryY generator. GEEs were fitted with geepack [25] with exchangeable, independence and first-order autoregressive (AR(1)) working correlations. They were combined with the uncorrected sandwich variance and with the corrections of Mancl and DeRouen [7], Kauermann and Carroll [8] and Fay and Graubard [9] (bound b = 0.75, as in [9]), computed with the R package fewclust (Table S2), written for this study and released with the code, which implements the published formulas and agreed with a computation by hand (Section S4). With exchangeable correlation, the Mancl-DeRouen and Fay-Graubard values in Table 3 and Table 4 were computed with geesmv [26], and those in Table 5 with fewclust (Section S4). The CR2 estimator of clubSandwich [27,28] was added with exchangeable and independence correlations. The mixed model was fitted with lme4::glmer [29] (Laplace approximation). After the main run, the mixed model with a random intercept was refitted by adaptive Gauss-Hermite quadrature with 10 nodes on a subset of null design points (Section 3.10). It had a random intercept in M1-M2 and the random slopes of the generating model in M3-M5. It was tested by a Wald test and by a likelihood-ratio test against the model without the interaction, with the same random effects. The shrinkage GLM rescales the mixed-model estimate and standard error by \((1 + k^2 D_{11})^{-1/2}\), with \(D_{11}\) the random-intercept variance. Software versions are in Table S2.

MMLB::mm writes the latent standard deviation as \(\exp(a_0) + \exp(a_1)\,t\), so a slope of zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space. In the main scenarios with a latent standard deviation that changes over time (M3-M5), the generating slope is close to that boundary. Without a check, two failure modes of the optimizer (nlm) produced excess rejections with long series: non-convergence, and convergence with a collapsed standard error. We therefore added a convergence check. A fit was declared at the boundary if nlm did not report convergence (return code other than 1 or 2) or if an estimated slope \(\exp(a_k)\) was below 0.001. Such a fit was replaced by the fit without the time trend of the latent standard deviation only if nlm reported convergence for that refit and its estimate and standard error were finite; otherwise the dataset gave no usable result for the marginalized model with the check. Section S20 compares this rule with versions that keep the original fit or accept a refit that did not converge.

Wald tests were referred to the standard normal in the primary tables and, as an alternative, to a t distribution with N - p degrees of freedom, p being the number of mean-model coefficients. The likelihood-ratio test was referred to a \(\chi^2\) distribution with one degree of freedom.

A sign-flip score test [30] was applied to every dataset. It treats subjects as independent units. With the other coefficients estimated, as here, the effective-score version is asymptotically exact and robust to differences in variance between subjects [30]; it is exact in finite samples only when no nuisance parameter is estimated and the contributions are symmetric. The test was declared not computable, and returned no answer, when the model without the interaction diverged (a coefficient of at least 1,000 in absolute value) or every score contribution was below \(10^{-6}\) in absolute value, because the interaction is then not identified. The test gives a p-value and no Wald interval; its computation and the interval obtained by inverting it are described in Section S7.

2.5 Performance measures

A replicate was usable for a Wald-based method when the fit returned without error and the estimate, its standard error and its p-value were finite, with |estimate| < 10 and \(0 <\) SE < 10. The likelihood-ratio test was usable when both fits converged and its p-value was finite, and the sign-flip test when it returned a finite p-value. A dataset in which every outcome took the same value, with no events or only events, gave no usable result for any method, whatever the fit returned; there were 9,711 such datasets among 4,752,000, 92% of them with two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters. Separated datasets, in which the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean model does not exist [31], were kept and judged by the same rule, because whether a method signals such data is a property an analyst needs to know; unlike a constant outcome, separation is not visible without a dedicated check. Detected by linear programming [32,33], they were 7.5% of the datasets with an estimable design and a non-constant outcome, 55% with two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters (Section S19). The probability of a usable result was computed under the null, at each design point, with every replicate with an estimable design (Section 2.2) in the denominator, including those whose fit failed; Table 4, Table 5 and the supplementary tables report its mean over design points. Fits that returned with warnings were kept (Table S13). Rates under the null and the alternative were computed on each method’s usable replicates, so a method that fails on difficult datasets is assessed on easier ones; the exception is the power of Table 5 and Table S31, computed per attempted dataset. Table S6 repeats the type I error on the replicates usable for all methods, and Table S9 by stratum of estimability.

Type I error was the rejection rate at the nominal 5% under H0. Over the grid we report the pooled rate and two summaries computed within each mechanism. A design point is a combination of scenario, mechanism, number of clusters and number of occasions; a cell is a design point under one hypothesis. For each of the 16 cluster counts we took the absolute departure from 5% of the replicate-weighted rate. The worst case is the largest of these absolute departures, and the mean absolute departure is their mean. By number of occasions (Section 3.1, Table S4) and in the direct comparison of the two strategies of the rule (Section 3.4, Figure 1, Table S31), the absolute departure is instead averaged over design points. At each design point, a strategy was clearly above 7.5% when the lower limit of the exact (Clopper-Pearson) 95% interval of its rejection rate exceeded 7.5%, and clearly below 2.5% when the upper limit fell below 2.5%; a design point with fewer than 20 usable null replicates was not assessed. These limits are Bradley’s liberal criterion, 0.5 to 1.5 times the nominal level [34]; for the coverage of 95% intervals they were applied to the rate of non-coverage. Unconditional validity is the probability of a usable result multiplied by the probability of not rejecting a true null given one. Power was reported raw and size-adjusted. Bias, empirical and model-based standard errors and coverage of the 95% interval were computed against the estimand of each method (Table S36).

Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE) were computed for every measure [21]. With 1,000 usable replicates, the MCSE of a rejection rate at 5% is 0.69 percentage points. This number of replicates was chosen so that a single cell resolves a departure from 5% of about 1.4 points. The datasets are common random numbers across cells. The MCSE of every summary over cells, and of every difference between methods, was therefore obtained by a bootstrap that resamples replicate indices jointly across all cells (2,000 resamples). A comparison between methods is written as a difference only when its bootstrap interval, the estimate ± 2 MCSE, lies entirely beyond a relevance margin fixed in advance. The margin is one percentage point for differences in type I error or coverage averaged over cells, 2.5 points for a single cell, two points for differences in power and 2.5 points for differences in usable shares. Intervals entirely within the margin are reported as similar. Intervals that straddle it are reported as differences of about the size of the margin.

2.6 Decision rule

The recommendation of Figure 1 comes from a rule applied to every strategy that returns an estimate and an interval, a strategy being a method with its reference distribution. A strategy was excluded if its type I error was clearly above 7.5% at any design point. With 1,000 usable replicates a design point is flagged only from an observed rate of 9.3%, and with half as many from 10%: a strategy never clearly above 7.5% is one in which no excess was detected, not one shown to be calibrated. Among the remaining strategies, the one that returned a usable result most often was recommended. The rule was applied to all 2,376 design points of the four mechanisms. The likelihood-ratio test and the sign-flip test give no interval and are reported for comparison. The strategy selected by the rule was then compared post hoc with GEE with an AR(1) working correlation, the Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference, which failed the rule at few design points (Section 3.4).

2.7 Clinical applications

The cohort comes from a prospective physiological study of neonates admitted to intensive care with respiratory failure [22]. It comprises 207 neonates with ten lung-ultrasound zones scored at one to three timepoints. It gives 230 patient-timepoints and 2,296 zone-level outcomes; 22 patients contribute more than one timepoint. The outcome is severe loss of aeration (prevalence 0.59). In a logistic mixed model of the outcome on zone region with a patient random intercept, the patient variance is 3.5. Adding a patient-timepoint level drives the patient variance to the boundary and places a variance of 3.8 at the new level (likelihood-ratio \(\chi^2\) = 47 on one degree of freedom). The contrast of interest is posterior against anterior zones, adjusted for disease, invasive ventilation and gestational age. It was estimated by the marginalized model, with a latent variable with an intercept only as in scenario M1 and a first-order transition term over the zones of each patient, by the GEEs and by the mixed model. With 207 clusters the cohort lies above the simulated range, so it was used as a plasmode. We drew 500 subsamples of whole patients at each of 10, 15, 20, 25 and 50 patients, with the full-cohort estimate of each method as its reference. In both applications the ratio of the mean standard error (model-based for the marginalized model and the mixed model, sandwich for the GEEs) to the standard deviation of the estimates over subsamples was multiplied by \(\sqrt{1 - N/P}\), with P the number of patients in the full dataset, because subsamples drawn without replacement from a finite cohort vary less than independent samples.

The same analysis was repeated on the respiratory trial distributed with geepack [25] (111 patients, four visits, active treatment against placebo). The contrast of interest was the treatment effect, adjusted for baseline status, visit, age, sex and centre.

3. Results

3.1 Type I error on the main grid

Table 3 gives the type I error of the eight methods on the 1,440 design points of the main grid with the first three mechanisms, under a normal reference, and Figure 2 shows the type I error of the eight methods at every design point, with the marginalized model highlighted. The pooled rejection rate of the marginalized model with the convergence check ranged from 5.1% to 5.3% across mechanisms. It ranged from 5.3% to 5.8% for Fay-Graubard and from 5.5% to 6.1% for Mancl-DeRouen. On GenBinaryY it reached 6.9% for Kauermann-Carroll and 8.4% for the uncorrected GEE.

The marginalized model had the smallest worst-case departure from 5% on all three mechanisms: 0.63, 0.5 and 0.43 percentage points on GenBinaryY, GLMM-native and GLMM-AR1, respectively. Its worst-case departure was smaller than that of the next method by 3.0 points on GenBinaryY and by about one point on the two random-effects mechanisms. Its mean absolute departure (0.20 to 0.33 points) and that of Fay-Graubard (0.52 to 1.0) were similar. On matched replicates usable for both methods, the two rejected a true null at similar rates.

The mean absolute departure of the marginalized model fell from 1.6 points at two occasions to 0.71 at four or more (Table S4). At two occasions the five marginal methods of Table 3 other than the shrinkage GLM departed by 1.6 to 2.6 points on average. The Wald test of the mixed model departed by 5.6 points, and the shrinkage GLM, which rescales it to a marginal estimand, by 11.

3.2 The convergence check of the marginalized model

In scenarios M3-M5 the check declared 71% of the null fits of the marginalized model at the boundary; it replaced 55% with the converged fit without the time trend of the latent standard deviation and left 16% (32% at two or three occasions) without a result. Without the check, the marginalized model was clearly above 7.5% at 149 of the 864 null design points of these scenarios, 90 of them with eight or ten occasions. With the check it was clearly above 7.5% at 0. Its mean absolute departure at ten occasions fell from 2.8 to 0.66 points.

In scenarios M6-M7 the fit without the time trend is misspecified. There the check declared 45% of the null fits at the boundary (64% at two or three occasions, where nlm most often failed to converge) and left 8.2% (18%) without a result. With a t reference, the marginalized model with the check was never clearly above 7.5% at the 384 design points. Without the check, and with a t reference, it was clearly above 7.5% at 9 design points. Bias, standard errors and coverage of the marginalized model with the check in these scenarios are in Section S13.

3.3 Availability of a result

The probability of a usable result depended mostly on the number of occasions (Table 4). With random slopes and two occasions, the mixed model returned a usable Wald test in 0.002% of attempts. The likelihood-ratio test with the same random effects was usable in 0.14%, against 42% for the marginalized model and 73% for Fay-Graubard. With random slopes the marginalized model returned a usable result in 69.1%, 80.6% and 90.4% of attempts at three, four and six occasions, against 87.1%, 92.9% and 97.4% with a random intercept only; a refit of its convergence check that does not converge leaves no result (Section 2.4). With a random intercept only, the likelihood-ratio test was usable in 99% of attempts at two occasions, against 69% for the Wald test. From four occasions every method returned a usable result in more than 80% of attempts.

At 20 clusters or fewer, unconditional validity ranged from 61% for the Wald test of the mixed model to 80% for the likelihood-ratio test (Table S8). A criterion that maximized unconditional validity at each cluster count would have selected the likelihood-ratio test up to 25 clusters on each of the three study mechanisms.

3.4 Reference distribution and the decision rule

Referring the Wald statistic to a t distribution with N - p degrees of freedom lowered every pooled rejection rate. The shift was 0.53 to 1.1 percentage points over the grid and 1.4 to 3.8 points at 25 clusters or fewer (Table S11). Under the t reference the marginalized model became conservative at ten clusters. There it was clearly below 2.5% at 26 of 102 design points, against 4 for Fay-Graubard.

Table 5 applies the rule of Section 2.6 to the 2,376 design points of the four mechanisms. Among the strategies with an interval, only the marginalized model with the check and a t reference was never clearly above 7.5%, and the rule selected it; it returned a usable result in 84% of datasets. GEE with AR(1) working correlation, Fay-Graubard and a t reference (the GEE strategy) returned a usable result more often, in 92%, a difference beyond the margin for usable shares (Section 2.5), but was clearly above 7.5% at 2 design points, both in scenario M2 with N = 10 and T = 2, on GLMM-AR1 and GLMM-native. There it rejected a true null in 12 of 61 and 11 of 63 usable replicates, the marginalized model in 0 of 35 and 0 of 38 (Section S10). Every one of these rejections fell on one of the 27 and 26 usable datasets with an infinite estimate of the interaction; on its other usable datasets it rejected 0 of 34 and 0 of 37. There the GEE estimate is where its iterations stopped: with 200 instead of 25 iterations it moved further from zero in 35 of 53. The marginalized model returned 4 usable results on such datasets in the whole study. If separated datasets gave no result to the strategies with an interval, the GEE strategy would be clearly above 7.5% at 0 design points and the rule would select it (Section S19). The choice rests on these two design points: with usability limits of 5 instead of 10 the GEE strategy was never clearly above 7.5% and the rule would have selected it, and with 20 it was clearly above 7.5% at 6 design points (Section S11). The GEE strategy was clearly below 2.5% at 106 design points and the marginalized model at 42, 32 of them at ten clusters.

With exchangeable or independence working correlation, Fay-Graubard with a t reference was clearly above 7.5% at 15 and 5 design points, 3 and 3 of them in the main grid, all with ten clusters and among them the two design points of the GEE strategy. Mancl-DeRouen with a t reference was clearly above 7.5% at 20 to 63 design points across working correlations, Kauermann-Carroll at 138 to 207, and the Wald test of the mixed model at 515, 55 of them on data generated by its own model (GLMM-native). The likelihood-ratio test was clearly above 7.5% at 412 design points.

With two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters, the GEE strategy and the marginalized model returned a usable result in fewer than half of the datasets (44% and 28%) and detected the simulated effect in fewer than 2% of attempted datasets (Table S31). With N - 2 degrees of freedom [15], on the 1,896 design points of the three study mechanisms, the rule selected the same strategy; the marginalized model was again never clearly above 7.5%, and clearly below 2.5% at 21 instead of 39 design points, and the GEE strategy was clearly above 7.5% at 2 (Table S26).

Compared directly, with the block bootstrap and the margins of Section 2.5 (Figure 1, Table S31), the marginalized model and the GEE strategy had similar mean absolute departures from 5% over all design points (1.2 and 1.1 percentage points) and similar power (difference 0.95 points), and the GEE strategy returned a usable result more often (difference 7.9 points). The GEE strategy was closer to 5% at ten clusters with three or more occasions (1.6 against 3.3 points), where the marginalized model was conservative (mean type I error 1.7% against 4.2%). With two occasions and 15 or more clusters the GEE strategy was conservative (2.5%), the two had similar mean absolute departures (difference 0.84 points), and the GEE strategy returned a usable result more often, by 21 points. With 15 or more clusters and three or more occasions the two were similar in level, and the GEE strategy answered more often by 4.6 points. With ten clusters and two occasions both answered rarely (in 10% and 4.3% of datasets) and both were far from 5% (mean absolute departures 5.4 and 5.1 points).

3.5 Working correlation and implementation of the corrections

Changing the working correlation of Fay-Graubard from exchangeable to independence or AR(1) changed its type I error by -0.29 and -0.31 percentage points on average over the 1,896 design points of the three study mechanisms, within the one-point margin. The two implementations of the corrections are compared in Section S4.

3.6 The fourth mechanism

On Copula-AR1 (480 design points) neither the GEE strategy nor the marginalized model with the check was clearly above 7.5% at any design point (Table 5). Their mean type I errors with a t reference were 4.6% and 4.9%, respectively. For both, the difference from the three study mechanisms was within the one-point margin. The Wald test of the mixed model (Laplace approximation) with a t reference rejected a true null in 10% of usable replicates on average, 3.2 points more than on the three study mechanisms, and was clearly above 7.5% at 223 of the 480 design points. GEE with exchangeable working correlation and Fay-Graubard was clearly above 7.5% at 8 design points, 6 with T = 4 and N = 10 to 25, and 2 with N = 10 and T = 3 or 6.

3.7 Sign-flip score test

Over the 2,376 design points the sign-flip test rejected a true null in 5.4% of datasets on average, and it was clearly above 7.5% or clearly below 2.5% at no design point. It answered in 97% of datasets with an estimable design and, with two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters, in 72%, against 44% for the GEE strategy (Table 5). Its type I error in those small designs was 5.2%, and its power per attempted dataset was 4.2% there and 21% over all design points. Inverted, the test gave an interval that covered the true value under the alternative in 95% of datasets, against 96% for the GEE strategy. In the small designs both of its ends were finite in 14% of datasets; its non-coverage was clearly below 2.5% at 97 design points, 90 of them with two occasions; and where both intervals existed it was 17% wider than the GEE interval on average over design points, less over datasets (Section S7, Table S27).

3.8 Power and coverage

Raw and size-adjusted power of the eight methods are in Table S10.

Coverage of the 95% interval was 94% to 95% for Fay-Graubard, Mancl-DeRouen and the marginalized model on every mechanism, and 93% to 94% for Kauermann-Carroll (Table S12).

3.9 Scenario anchored to the cohort

Scenario M1c has the prevalence and between-subject variance of the cohort (72 design points). Under a normal reference the marginalized model rejected a true null in 6.8% to 7.0% of usable replicates, against 5.0% to 5.1% for Fay-Graubard. Its worst-case departure was larger than that of the best method by about the one-point margin. Under a t reference its rate was 5.0% to 5.1%, and that of Fay-Graubard 3.5% to 3.6%.

3.10 Adaptive quadrature for the mixed model

The refit covered 123 null design points: N ∈ {10, 25, 55, 145} and T ∈ {2, 4, 10} in M1 and M2, and N ∈ {10, 25, 45} and T ∈ {2, 4, 6} in M1c (Section S12, Table S34). With a t reference, on the replicates usable under both fits, quadrature lowered the rejection rate under the null by 3.1 to 4.0 percentage points on average, depending on the mechanism. The Wald test was clearly above 7.5% at 33 of these design points under the Laplace approximation and at 8 with quadrature, all with T = 10: 6 on Copula-AR1 (12% to 16%) and 2 on GenBinaryY (9.3% and 9.6%). On data generated by its own model it was no longer clearly above 7.5% at any of them. Quadrature also made the test conservative, mostly with few clusters: it was clearly below 2.5% at 37 design points, against 3 under the Laplace approximation (Table S34).

3.11 Clinical applications

In the full cohort the posterior-versus-anterior contrast was 0.35 (SE 0.10) by the marginalized model and 0.38 (SE 0.17) by GEE with an exchangeable working correlation and the uncorrected sandwich. The mixed model gave 0.48 (SE 0.12) on its conditional scale. In subsamples of 10 patients, 22% of draws contained no invasively ventilated patient, so that the mean model could not be fitted (Table S15). Over all subsamples of this size, including those, a usable result was obtained by the mixed model in 78%, by the marginalized model in 77%, by the uncorrected GEE in 70%, by Fay-Graubard in 34% and by Mancl-DeRouen in 15%. Most failures of the corrections returned a point estimate without a standard error (Table S15). Across subsample sizes, after the finite-population correction, the standard error of the mixed model was 0.51 to 0.58 times the empirical standard deviation of its estimates. The corresponding ratio was 0.56 to 0.62 for the marginalized model, and 0.85 to 0.99 with its robust standard error (Section S9).

In the respiratory trial the treatment effect was 1.3 (SE 0.34) by the marginalized model and 1.3 by GEE with an exchangeable working correlation (SE 0.35 uncorrected, 0.35 to 0.37 with the three corrections; Table S29), and 2.1 on the conditional scale of the mixed model. In subsamples of 10 patients, with the full mean model, a usable result was returned by the mixed model in 53% of draws, by the marginalized model in 50%, by the uncorrected GEE in 47%, by Fay-Graubard in 23% and by Mancl-DeRouen in 23%; as in the cohort, the corrections mostly failed with an estimate but no standard error (Table S30).

4. Discussion

4.1 The recommendation

One strategy met the rule of Section 2.6: the marginalized model with the convergence check and a t reference (Figure 1). Across the 2,376 design points of the four mechanisms it was never clearly above 7.5%, and it returned a usable result in 84% of datasets. GEE with an AR(1) working correlation, the Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference with N - p degrees of freedom failed the rule at 2 design points, both with ten clusters and two occasions, and returned a usable result more often, in 92% (with an independence working correlation Fay-Graubard was clearly above 7.5% at 5 design points). The margin between the two is narrow: the failure rests on two design points where both answered rarely, on datasets in which the estimate does not exist, and it disappears with a stricter usability limit (Section 3.4). In the direct comparison, which was not pre-specified, the two had similar level and power, and the GEE strategy answered more often. We therefore present it as a simpler alternative, which needs no convergence check, outside designs with ten clusters and two occasions and after a check for separation. Where the two differed in level beyond the margin, at ten clusters with three or more occasions, it was the one closer to nominal; with two occasions and 15 or more clusters it is conservative. Because the fourth mechanism has AR(1) dependence on the latent scale, it could favour the AR(1) working correlation. The working correlation changed the level of Fay-Graubard by less than half a point on average, and the rule made the same choice on the three study mechanisms alone (Table S26). The R package fewclust (version 0.4.2), written for this study, applies this recommendation: it fits the marginalized model with the convergence check and a t reference, and the GEE strategy when the marginalized model returns no usable result, and it stops with an explanation when the mean model is separated. By default it also treats as not converged a fit with a trend of the latent standard deviation whose log-likelihood is below that of the fit without the trend; this condition is not part of the rule, and on 125 datasets regenerated from the study it changed the reported fit in 4.

The two failures of the GEE strategy came from data without information about the interaction, which are common in small designs (Section 2.5). There GEE returned a plausible estimate and standard error with no sign of the problem, whereas the marginalized model almost never returned a result (Section 3.4). We therefore advise checking for separation before reporting a GEE analysis with few clusters, for example with the R package detectseparation [33], and, when the data are separated, not reporting a Wald test of the separated coefficient or using a penalized likelihood [31].

The rule asks that a recommendation hold at every design point, because an analyst knows the number of clusters and occasions but not the mechanism that generated the data. It replaces a criterion that maximized unconditional validity at each cluster count. That criterion rewards a method for answering, whatever its level. On the present data it would have recommended the likelihood-ratio test of the mixed model up to 25 clusters, a test that was clearly above 7.5% at 412 design points. Fay-Graubard with an exchangeable working correlation would not have met the rule: with a t reference it was clearly above 7.5% at 15 design points, 4 in scenarios M6-M7 and 8 on the fourth mechanism (Table 5).

With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters, no strategy with an interval among those evaluated was both available and calibrated. The recommended strategy and the GEE strategy returned a usable result in fewer than half of the datasets and detected the simulated effect in fewer than 2% of attempted datasets. The sign-flip test answered in 72% of those datasets and kept its level, but it detected the simulated effect in only 4.2% of attempted datasets: it gives a valid test where the estimators return nothing, not a powerful one. Inverting it gives an interval whose coverage rests on unbounded intervals in those designs (Section 3.7). We therefore do not propose it as an interval to use. With a random slope and two occasions, the random-effects covariance of the mixed model is not identifiable, since two subject-level parameters saturate two observations, and its Wald test was essentially never usable. The case for the maximal random-effects structure [35] is thus bounded by power [36] and, with two occasions, by identifiability. In these designs, what can be learned depends more on the number of occasions and clusters than on the analysis. Four or more occasions per subject, or more clusters, should be planned where possible.

4.2 The convergence check

The check addresses a property of the parametrization rather than of the marginalized model. Because the slope is exponentiated, a slope near zero lies on the boundary, where nlm fails in the two ways described in Section 2.4. Replacing such fits with the converged fit without the time trend, and giving no result when that fit did not converge, removed the excess. The cost is availability (Section 3.2): accepting a refit that did not converge would raise the usable share in Table 5 to 91%, and keeping the original fit would leave the model clearly above 7.5% at 4 design points (Section S20). In M6-M7, where the reasons were recorded, the check intervened with two or three occasions mostly because nlm did not converge. Where it intervened, the type I error stayed close to nominal. It also remained calibrated in M6-M7, where the fit without the time trend is misspecified. Analysts who use the marginalized model with a latent standard deviation that changes over time should apply the check and report how often it intervened and how often it left no result.

4.3 Relation to previous work

We reproduce the anticonservatism of the uncorrected sandwich with few clusters [7,8]. As in stepped-wedge trials with binary outcomes, where Fay-Graubard and an approximation to Kauermann-Carroll performed best [18], Fay-Graubard with a t reference was the correction that best kept the level here. A systematic review of parallel cluster-randomized trials recommended it for continuous outcomes, and for binary outcomes the mixed model with a between-within correction or Mancl-DeRouen [16]. Li and Redden found that Kauermann-Carroll attains the nominal level at ten clusters under a t reference [15]. In our data, with the correction computed from its published formula, its rate at ten clusters under a t reference was 9.4% to 12%, above Bradley’s limit, and over the four mechanisms it was clearly above 7.5% at 138 to 207 of 2,376 design points across working correlations. Their trials had low intracluster correlation, large clusters, a cluster-level treatment and K - 2 degrees of freedom [15], so the difference may reflect the design rather than the estimator. Our Kauermann-Carroll values come from fewclust, which agreed with a computation by hand (Section S4); geesmv computes a different quantity (Section S4), and Thompson et al. also reported unstable Kauermann-Carroll standard errors from it [18], so published values obtained with it are not directly comparable with ours. Mancl and DeRouen reported sizes close to nominal with ten subjects [7], and Bie et al. favoured GEE with the Mancl-DeRouen correction [19]. Under a t reference its pooled rate here was 4.7% to 5.3%, inside Bradley’s limits. With exchangeable working correlation it was nevertheless clearly above 7.5% at 63 design points, 18 of them in scenarios M6-M7 and 28 on the fourth mechanism. With few clusters, Bie et al. found the standard error of the marginalized model nearly correct for within-cluster contrasts, as here, but too small for between-cluster ones [19]. McNeish preferred restricted penalized quasi-likelihood with a Kenward-Roger correction to quadrature for mixed logistic models with few clusters, especially with many observations per cluster [37]; it was not evaluated here.

4.4 The clinical applications and the fourth mechanism

In both applications the model-based standard errors of the mixed model and of the marginalized model fell short of the spread of their estimates at every subsample size, by similar amounts (Section 3.11, Section S9, Table S30). The robust standard error of the marginalized model was close to the spread in the cohort but not in the trial with few patients (Section S9). In the trial, with seven mean-model coefficients and few patients, the estimates are unstable, and their spread may be inflated by large estimates that the usability filter keeps. On the fourth mechanism with ten occasions, the excess rejection of the mixed model persisted under adaptive quadrature. It is consistent with its standard error, which under the Laplace approximation, with a random intercept and 85 or more clusters, was on average 0.64 to 0.81 times the spread of its estimates under the null (Section S8), and with a random intercept that ignores the stronger correlation between neighbouring occasions. Elsewhere much of its excess came from the Laplace approximation, which is inaccurate with few binary observations per cluster [37].

4.5 Limitations

In the main scenarios the random-slope variance and the time trend of the latent standard deviation were small. Conclusions about random slopes therefore rest mainly on scenarios M6-M7, which cover one structure (a slope on time) and two mechanisms. Trends of the latent standard deviation between those of the main scenarios (0.01 per occasion) and of M6 (0.1) were not simulated; reporting how often the check intervenes (Section 4.2) is the safeguard. The number of occasions observed did not depend on the outcomes, so informative dropout was not studied, and the results concern a linear treatment-by-time interaction. Three working correlations were compared; a misspecified variance function was not simulated. The AR(1) working correlation is safe here because the mean at each occasion depended only on the current values of time and dose; when it depends on covariate values at other occasions, for example through lagged effects of a time-varying exposure, a working correlation other than independence can bias the GEE estimate [38,39]. Three of the four mechanisms contain a component that is constant within subject, and two of them are the home models of the marginalized model and of the mixed model. No mechanism had a random-effect variance that differed between arms, under which the marginalized model was biased in a previous study, where it was robust to non-normal random effects [19]. The fourth has only serial dependence (Section 4.1). In a replication of the study, the marginalized model could be clearly above 7.5% at one or more design points (in 58% of bootstrap resamples), and the GEE strategy almost always would be (in 99%). In the bootstrap, in the plug-in calculation and with the rates shrunk by empirical Bayes (Table S37), the marginalized model had the fewest expected design points clearly above 7.5% (Section S11). In GLMM-native the marginal value under the null is not exactly zero. The excess rejection it can cause is at most 0.029 percentage points in the main scenarios and 0.26 in M6-M7 for the marginalized model and the GEEs, and subtracting it changes none of the flags clearly above 7.5% or clearly below 2.5% of these methods. The convergence check was introduced after part of the results had been seen, and was then tested on scenarios simulated afterwards. The decision rule itself replaced the criterion of an earlier version after that version’s results had been seen, and the direct comparison of the marginalized model with the GEE strategy was not pre-specified. The tables report the mixed model fitted by the Laplace approximation, the default of lme4; adaptive quadrature, which lme4 offers only with a single random intercept, was examined after the main run on a subset of design points (Section 3.10) and could not be examined with random slopes. Penalized GEE [14], the Morel correction [11], the degrees of freedom proposed with the Fay-Graubard correction [9] and penalized quasi-likelihood for the mixed model [37] were not evaluated; the average of the Mancl-DeRouen and Kauermann-Carroll variances [13] was evaluated and failed the rule (Section S6). Treatment was assigned by simple randomization with probability one half, so with ten subjects some datasets had unbalanced arms, and datasets with a degenerate design were excluded. The AR(1) and independence versions of the corrections, including the GEE strategy, and Kauermann-Carroll rest on one implementation (fewclust), checked against a computation by hand (Section S4). The clinical applications use two datasets with one outcome each. The subsampling resamples whole patients, and in the neonatal cohort the patient-timepoint level that carries most of the dependence is identified by only 22 patients measured more than once.

5. Conclusions

With few clusters and short series, the choice of analysis for a clustered binary outcome decides whether the test keeps its nominal level and whether it returns an answer at all. The marginalized multilevel model fitted with a convergence check and a t reference was never clearly above 7.5% at any simulated design point of four mechanisms. GEE with an AR(1) working correlation, the Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference was clearly above 7.5% only at two design points with ten clusters and two occasions, where all its false positives came from separated datasets on which it returned plausible estimates. Elsewhere its calibration differed from that of the marginalized model beyond the relevance margin only at ten clusters, where it was closer to nominal. The Wald test of the mixed model fitted by the Laplace approximation was anticonservative; with adaptive quadrature, examined for a random intercept, the excess remained only with ten occasions, mainly under serial dependence, and with few clusters the test became conservative. With two or three occasions and up to 25 clusters, neither strategy returned a usable result in half of the datasets. A sign-flip score test can still test for an effect there, with little power, and none of the analyses evaluated estimates the effect reliably; in that regime the design limits what any analysis can show.

In the designs studied, for a within-subject treatment-by-time interaction, we recommend the marginalized multilevel model with the convergence check and a t reference with N - p degrees of freedom, the only strategy that met the decision rule. GEE with an AR(1) working correlation, the Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference is a simpler alternative, which needs no convergence check, returns a result more often and was closer to nominal at ten clusters with three or more occasions, but not with ten clusters and two occasions; it should be preceded by a check for separation.

Code and data availability

The simulation code, the per-replicate results and the scripts that produce every number, table and figure of this paper are available in a public repository, together with the R package fewclust written for this study, which implements the recommended strategy (Section 4.1); the link and the archived version are withheld for anonymized review and given on the title page. The manuscript source reads every number in the text from a registry of values, each with its source file and checksum. The clinical cohort cannot be shared publicly; the plasmode results are included as summary tables. The respiratory trial data are distributed with the R package geepack [25].

Figure 1. Recommended analysis for the test of the treatment-by-time interaction with few clusters. (a) Comparison of the two strategies in each region of clusters and occasions, by the difference in mean absolute departure from the nominal 5% (block bootstrap; Table S31): the strategy is named where it is closer by more than the one-point margin of Section 2.5 over the whole interval, “GEE = MMM” elsewhere, with a dotted frame where the interval crosses the margin; “usable”: datasets returning a usable result (%), GEE/MMM. MMM = marginalized multilevel model with the convergence check and a t reference with N - p degrees of freedom, the recommended strategy; GEE = AR(1) working correlation, Fay-Graubard correction and a t reference, the simpler alternative, clearly above 7.5% at two design points with ten clusters and two occasions; N = number of clusters, p = number of mean-model coefficients. Dashed frame: two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters, where on average both answer in fewer than half the datasets (Table 5) and the sign-flip test is a complement. (b) Mean absolute departure from the nominal 5% (percentage points) by number of occasions, over the 2,376 design points of the four mechanisms (likelihood-ratio test: the 2,094 design points at which it returned at least one usable result), logarithmic axis. (c) Percentage of design points at which each strategy is clearly above 7.5% (exact 95% interval), by number of clusters (Table 5). (d) Mean absolute departure from 5% of the two strategies by number of clusters, with two occasions (dashed) and three or more (solid). (e) Datasets returning a usable result (%) and (f) datasets in which the simulated effect was detected, among those attempted (%), by number of occasions, for the two strategies and the sign-flip test. Wald tests with a t reference, likelihood-ratio test with a \(\chi^2\) reference. Bars in (b) and (d): estimate ± 2 Monte Carlo standard errors by block bootstrap, for the two strategies. AR(1) = first-order autoregressive working correlation, exch. = exchangeable, FG = Fay-Graubard, MD = Mancl-DeRouen, LRT = likelihood-ratio test of the GLMM, MMM = marginalized multilevel model.

Figure 2. Type I error at every design point of the main grid and M1c (nested-loop plot) for the eight methods of Table 3, Wald tests with a normal reference and the likelihood-ratio test with a \(\chi^2\) reference. Highlighted: the marginalized model with the convergence check (MMM), GEE with exchangeable working correlation and the Fay-Graubard correction (FG) and the likelihood-ratio test of the GLMM (LRT); grey: the uncorrected GEE (GEE), the Mancl-DeRouen (MD) and Kauermann-Carroll (KC) corrections, the Wald test of the GLMM (GLMM) and the shrinkage GLM (Shrink). Design points are ordered by scenario (outer loop), number of occasions T and number of clusters N (inner loop, bottom panel); rows are the mechanisms. Grey band: 2.5% to 7.5%; line: nominal 5%. Points with fewer than 20 usable replicates are not drawn and the axis is truncated at 30%. The Monte Carlo standard error of a rate of 5% is 0.69 points with 1,000 usable replicates and at most 6.4 points at any drawn design point.
